<reason>CON built a tighter, more sustained case around a single load-bearing pressure point: the five coastal states who would have to ratify any Arctic treaty explicitly rejected the model at Ilulissat in 2008, and nothing since has softened that (if anything, Ukraine-era hardening cuts the other way). PRO's answer to this in Rebuttal 2 and the pressure round ("deadlock itself forces yes") was asserted rather than mechanistically supported, and PRO's closing pivoted to a "what rules reward" reframe instead of shoring up the achievability answer, effectively leaving CON's central pressure question live at the end. CON also paired the feasibility attack with concrete, plausible existing-law counter-examples (CLCS adjudication, the 2010 Barents Sea resolution, the Polar Code, narrow search-and-rescue/spill deals) that did double duty: they answered PRO's Q1 about who gets the Ridge and undercut the "necessity" half of PRO's case by showing functional governance already exists without demanding a sovereignty/deterrence-threatening treaty. PRO's strongest material—the incentive-to-race framing and the sharp closing line that "deterrence does not freeze; it arms"—was rhetorically effective and genuinely engaged CON's "deterrence already freezes escalation" claim, but it arrived only in PRO's closing, after CON's Rebuttal 2, and CON's final closing (which had the last word) was not required to address it since the format allows crystallizing existing clash rather than opening new exchanges. Both sides followed the Q/A format correctly, but CON's answers were more concrete and left fewer open threads, while PRO's core achievability gap was never closed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Answer 1 in Rebuttal 2 (citing CLCS adjudication and the actual 2010 Russia-Norway Barents Sea settlement) directly answered PRO's pressure question about who gets the Ridge, converting an abstract "race to the bottom" worry into a concrete counter-example of the current system working, which PRO never fully neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
